reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Defined by the sequential or simultaneous involvement of two or more named peripheral nerves in different limbs, producing an asymmetric, patchy deficit
The stepwise, painful onset of individual nerve territories is an important clue that separates it from length-dependent symmetrical neuropathy
Vasculitis is a leading cause, so systemic features such as weight loss, rash, arthralgia, and renal involvement should be sought
Diabetes mellitus is a common metabolic cause and may combine several mechanisms
As lesions accumulate they can become confluent and mimic a symmetrical polyneuropathy, obscuring the underlying pattern
Nerve conduction studies show a multifocal, often axonal process with asymmetry between nerves
Nerve biopsy, typically of the sural nerve, may be needed to confirm vasculitis and guide immunosuppression
Because vasculitic neuropathy reflects ischaemic nerve infarction, prompt recognition and treatment can prevent irreversible axonal loss
reference.pathophysiology: Mononeuritis multiplex arises from multifocal damage to individual peripheral nerves, most classically through occlusion or inflammation of the vasa nervorum (nerve ischaemia) in systemic or non-systemic vasculitis. Ischaemic infarction of nerve fascicles produces predominantly axonal loss in the territories supplied by affected vessels, explaining the patchy, asymmetric deficits. Other mechanisms include direct infiltration, compression at multiple sites, immune-mediated demyelination, and metabolic injury as in diabetes. The random distribution reflects the scattered nature of the underlying microvascular or infiltrative lesions.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic vasculitides (polyarteritis nodosa, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis)
Multiple compressive mononeuropathies (including hereditary neuropathy with pressure palsies)
Infective causes such as leprosy, HIV, and Lyme disease
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to map the multifocal, asymmetric pattern
Inflammatory and autoimmune screen (ESR, CRP, ANCA, ANA, complement, cryoglobulins)
Testing for diabetes, HIV, hepatitis B and C, and other infective causes
Nerve and muscle biopsy to confirm vasculitis when systemic markers are inconclusive
Assessment for systemic organ involvement including renal function and urinalysis
Imaging or further workup for sarcoidosis or malignancy when suspected
redFlags: Rapidly progressive multifocal deficits with systemic features suggesting active vasculitis requiring urgent immunosuppression
Evidence of multi-organ involvement such as renal impairment, pulmonary haemorrhage, or gut ischaemia
Severe constitutional symptoms indicating an aggressive systemic process
New motor deficits threatening limb function that demand expedited diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the underlying cause and the speed of treatment; vasculitic cases can recover substantially if immunosuppression is started before extensive axonal infarction, but delayed treatment or severe systemic disease leaves persistent deficits.
pitfalls: Waiting for a symmetrical pattern to emerge and missing the early asymmetric vasculitic phase
Attributing the picture to diabetes alone without excluding treatable vasculitis
Delaying nerve biopsy and immunosuppression when vasculitis is clinically likely
Overlooking systemic organ involvement that alters urgency and prognosis
Failing to consider infective causes such as leprosy in appropriate settings
management: Treat the underlying cause, with corticosteroids plus immunosuppression such as cyclophosphamide or rituximab for vasculitis, tight glycaemic control for diabetic disease, and targeted antimicrobial or antiviral therapy for infective causes
Tailor immunomodulation to aetiology, for example intravenous immunoglobulin for immune-mediated disease and treatment of cryoglobulinaemia or underlying hepatitis
Neuropathic pain management with agents such as gabapentinoids or tricyclic antidepressants
Rehabilitation with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, orthoses such as a foot-drop splint, and falls prevention
Monitor disease activity, treatment toxicity and end-organ involvement, with surveillance for relapse
Escalate immunosuppression promptly for progressive deficit to prevent irreversible axonal infarction, within multidisciplinary neurology and rheumatology care
